corrected_answer:
STANCE 200 - Separate the three claims RDMA bundles together, since kernel bypass, zero copy and offloaded transport fail independently and are measured differently.

Mechanism. RDMA is usually presented as one property but delivers three: the data path avoids kernel involvement, payloads are not copied into intermediate buffers, and the transport runs on the adapter rather than on host cores. A deployment can obtain one without the others, for example by registering memory correctly but still copying at the application layer, and the resulting performance looks like RDMA failing when it is in fact partially bypassed.

Falsifiable hypothesis. H1: host CPU time per transferred byte falls to near zero and copy counts on the data path are zero, so all three properties are active rather than only the transport offload. Falsified if CPU time per byte remains comparable to the socket baseline, which indicates the application is still copying and the bypass is not reaching the payload.

Metrics. Host CPU cycles per transferred byte, memory copies observed on the data path, achieved bandwidth against link rate, completion latency distribution, and the equivalent figures for a socket baseline on the same hardware. All of these are MEASURED against the socket baseline; any bandwidth figure quoted from adapter specifications rather than from the deployment is an ESTIMATE and should not be used for planning.

Controlled experiment. Run identical transfer sizes over the RDMA path and a socket path on the same hosts and links, reporting all three properties separately rather than reporting end-to-end bandwidth alone, since bandwidth can be adequate while CPU cost is unchanged.

Confounders. Memory registration cost is paid once and is invisible in steady-state measurements while dominating short-lived connections. Some stacks silently fall back to a copy path when registration fails, which looks like working RDMA at lower speed.

Rollback criteria. If the CPU-per-byte property is absent, fix the application data path rather than tuning transport parameters. Treat any RDMA benefit claim without a same-hardware socket baseline as unsupported and do not carry it into a capacity plan.

corrected_answer:
STANCE 201 - Measure the completion latency distribution rather than the mean, because collective performance is set by the slowest participant.

Mechanism. A collective operation completes when its last participant completes, so the operation's latency tracks the tail of the per-link distribution rather than its mean. An interconnect change that improves mean latency while widening the tail can make collectives slower, and a mean-only measurement will report the change as an improvement.

Falsifiable hypothesis. H1: collective completion time correlates with the tail of the per-link completion distribution and not with its mean, so the tail is the quantity that must be optimised. Falsified if collective time tracks the mean and is insensitive to the tail, which would indicate the collective is bandwidth-bound rather than synchronisation-bound at this message size.

Metrics. Full per-operation completion latency distribution including high percentiles, collective completion time, per-rank arrival skew at the collective, and message size. Distributions are MEASURED per rank; attributing collective slowdown to a specific link is an ESTIMATE unless per-link counters are collected simultaneously.

Controlled experiment. Sweep message size across the range where the collective transitions from latency-bound to bandwidth-bound, recording the full distribution at each size, so the regime is identified rather than assumed.

Confounders. Rank arrival skew from unrelated compute imbalance produces the same signature as network tail latency and must be separated by timestamping arrival at the collective. Background traffic on shared links varies with cluster occupancy.

Rollback criteria. Revert any interconnect or firmware change that widens the tail even if the mean improves, and record the tail percentile the decision was made on so later comparisons use the same statistic.

corrected_answer:
STANCE 202 - Confirm the path in use before attributing results to it, because silent fallback to a slower transport is the common explanation for absent gains.

Mechanism. Communication libraries select a transport at initialisation and fall back when a requirement is unmet, often logging at a verbosity that is disabled by default. A deployment can therefore be running over a TCP path while every configuration file names RDMA. Verifying the selected transport from runtime output and adapter counters must precede any performance interpretation.

Falsifiable hypothesis. H1: adapter-level counters account for the transferred bytes, confirming traffic traverses the intended path rather than a fallback. Falsified if adapter counters show negligible traffic while the application transfers data, which localises the problem to transport selection rather than to tuning.

Metrics. Bytes reported by adapter counters against bytes transferred by the application, the transport named in initialisation output, and the count of fallback events logged at increased verbosity. Counter agreement is MEASURED; a transport named in configuration but not confirmed by counters is an ESTIMATE of what the system is doing and is frequently wrong.

Controlled experiment. Enable the communication library's transport-selection logging, run a fixed transfer, and reconcile application bytes against adapter counters, treating any material discrepancy as the finding rather than proceeding to tuning.

Confounders. Multiple adapters may be present and counters read from the wrong one show no traffic. Container network namespaces can hide the adapter from the counter query while the transfer still uses it.

Rollback criteria. Stop performance work until the path is confirmed, since every measurement before that point describes an unknown configuration. Record the verification output alongside any published result so the path is auditable later.

corrected_answer:
DUPLICATE OF FAMILY 514 - no additional supervision signal; recommend removal from the training mixture.

Finding. This record is one of 109 rows in train.jsonl whose user turn differs from the others only by a variant number and whose assistant turn is byte-identical across the whole family. Reviewing it as an independent item would require inventing a distinct answer for a question that has already been answered, which manufactures stylistic variety rather than domain signal.

Retained exemplars. corpus-05001, corpus-05002, corpus-05003. Those records carry the substantive review for this family; this record adds nothing beyond them.

Why duplicates are harmful here. Under a fixed step budget every duplicate consumes an optimiser step, so a family of 109 rows receives roughly 109 times the weight of a singleton family. That concentrates training on one question and its single rubric answer, and if that answer is defective the defect is amplified rather than averaged away. The source assistant turn here is a grading rubric rather than an answer, so the amplified content is a description of what a good answer would contain instead of the answer itself.

Recommended action. Drop this record from the supervised mixture and retain the exemplars. If variety within the family is wanted, generate it from distinct underlying scenarios with distinct reference answers rather than by renumbering a variant, because renumbering changes the prompt without changing the supervision target.

Evidence label. The family size and the byte-identity of the assistant turns are MEASURED by grouping train.jsonl; no ESTIMATE is involved in this decision.
